F–E–F–D: four notes that can bring death into a piece before a word is sung. The medieval Dies irae chant tells of the Day of Judgement. Later composers carry its opening into symphonies and dances, where the old tune can terrify or grin.

B♭–A–C–B♮ spells Bach in German note names. He writes that signature into the third subject of his unfinished fugue in The Art of Fugue. Later composers take the four notes as a challenge: a name that can be turned upside down, woven into a fugue or carried into new harmony.

F–B–D♯–G♯ sounds in bar 2 of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde prelude. The chord promises a resolution that the music keeps postponing. Its four notes came to stand for longing itself, ready for later composers to quote with devotion or a sly smile.

The bass falls through a fourth and starts again. In Purcell’s When I am laid in earth, it fills the descent from G to D with every semitone while Dido sings her farewell. Her phrases change; the bass keeps coming back.

An old dance tune and a familiar round of chords leave plenty of room for mischief. Vivaldi begins his Folia in D minor, the first violin stepping slowly through the tune. The variations soon set the fingers running.
